Shoot
SHOOT
v.t. & v.i.
From Anglo-Saxon sceotan, to dart or send forth swiftly. Webster 1828: to let fly and drive with force, as an arrow from a bow. The Psalms use it of the wicked ambushing the upright, of God answering them in kind, and of a gesture of contempt made at the cross.

Biblical Definition

Psalm 11 describes the tactic of the wicked with precision, and the operative word is privily: lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart (Psalm 11:2). Preparation, concealment, and a specific target. Psalm 64 answers with the same verb turned round, and the reversal is exact: But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded (Psalm 64:7) — they prepared in secret and God is sudden. The word also names a gesture. In the psalm our Lord quoted from the cross, the mockers do something with the mouth that is hard to render and easy to picture: All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head (Psalm 22:7) — and Matthew 27:39 records the head-shaking at Calvary. Jonathan uses the word for the signal that saved David’s life: I will shoot three arrows on the side thereof, as though I shot at a mark (1 Samuel 20:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines SHOOT as to let fly and drive with force; to discharge, as an arrow or a bullet; to send out or forth; to push out, as a bud or branch.

expand to see more

SHOOT, v.t. — To let fly and drive with force; as, to shoot an arrow.

To discharge and cause to be driven with violence; as, to shoot a gun.

To send out or forth; to emit; as, to shoot forth rays.

SHOOT, v.i. — To germinate; to bud; to sprout; to push out, as a plant.

Anglo-Saxon sceotan, to dart forth — the root of shot, sheet and shut.

Key Scripture

Psalm 11:2 — "For, lo, the wicked bend their bow, they make ready their arrow upon the string, that they may privily shoot at the upright in heart."

Psalm 64:7 — "But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded."

Psalm 22:7 — "All they that see me laugh me to scorn: they shoot out the lip, they shake the head, saying,"

1 Samuel 20:20 — "And I will shoot three arrows on the side thereof, as though I shot at a mark."

Modern Corruption

Psalm 22 is quoted by Christ from the cross and its details are fulfilled at Calvary, which the critical habit of treating messianic psalms as retrofitted after the fact cannot honestly explain.

expand to see more

Psalm 22 opens with the words our Lord cried from the cross and proceeds through a series of details the Gospels record: the mocking and head-shaking (Psalm 22:7; Matthew 27:39), the taunt He trusted on the LORD that he would deliver him (Psalm 22:8; Matthew 27:43), the pierced hands and feet (Psalm 22:16), the bones out of joint, the tongue cleaving to the jaws, and the parting of garments with lots cast for the vesture (Psalm 22:18; John 19:24). The standard critical treatment reduces these to a sufferer’s generic lament that the evangelists later mined for correspondences. That explanation must account for a psalm written centuries before crucifixion was practised, describing pierced hands and feet and a division of clothing by lot, and closing with a declaration to a people yet unborn. This dictionary holds predictive prophecy as prophecy, and treats the Gospels’ use of the psalm as identification rather than invention.

Psalm 11 and Psalm 64 belong together as a pair on the manner of malice. The wicked prepare, string the arrow, and shoot privily — concealment is part of the method, and the whole force of Psalm 11 is that the righteous man is advised to flee and answers that he trusts in the LORD. God’s response in Psalm 64 uses the same weapon and reverses the timing: they were secret, He is sudden. The pattern is worth holding on to when a believer is under a campaign he cannot see the shape of. Scripture does not promise the arrows will miss; it says the LORD is in His holy temple, His eyes behold, His eyelids try the children of men (Psalm 11:4), and the outcome is His to arrange.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yarah (H3384), to shoot or cast, the same root that gives torah, teaching aimed at a mark; chets (H2671), an arrow; pathar (H6362), to open, of the lip.

expand to see more

Hebrew yarah (H3384) — to cast or shoot; the root also of torah, instruction, as an arrow aimed at a target.

Hebrew chets (H2671) — an arrow; God shall shoot at them with an arrow (Psalm 64:7).

Hebrew pathar (H6362) — to open or separate; they shoot out the lip, a gesture of derision (Psalm 22:7).

Hebrew sethar (H5643) — secrecy, concealment; privily shoot at the upright in heart (Psalm 11:2).

Hebrew nua (H5128) — to shake or wag; they shake the head (Psalm 22:7).

Usage

"That they may privily shoot at the upright in heart (Psalm 11:2) — preparation, concealment, a specific target."

"But God shall shoot at them with an arrow; suddenly shall they be wounded (Psalm 64:7) — they were secret; He is sudden."

"They shoot out the lip, they shake the head (Psalm 22:7) — the gesture recorded again at Calvary."
